title: Song of Solomon Is Far More Sensual Than Many Christians Were Told
paragraphs:
Song of Solomon Is Far More Sensual Than Many Christians Were Told
The Bible did not blush when it spoke about married desire. We did. And somewhere between shame, silence, pornography, purity, longing, and grace, many Christians stopped hearing what this astonishing book was actually saying.
There is a book in your Bible that some Christians almost seem embarrassed to read out loud.
Not because it describes war.
Not because somebody gets murdered.
Not because a prophet announces judgment.
Because a woman says she wants the man she loves to kiss her.
Because a man looks at the woman he loves and notices her body.
Because she notices his.
Because they desire one another.
Because Scripture sometimes speaks about human sexuality without sounding ashamed that God created human beings with bodies.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable part is this:
God allowed those words to remain in His Word.
“The Song of Songs, which is Solomon’s. Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth…”
That is essentially how the book begins.
Not with an apology.
Not with embarrassment.
With longing.
The Hebrew is striking:
יִשָּׁקֵנִי מִנְּשִׁיקוֹת פִּיהוּ
Yishaqeni minneshiqot pihu.
“Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth.”
She speaks first.
Sit with that.

The woman is not merely the passive object of male attraction. She possesses a voice. Longing. Affection. Agency. She knows whom she loves, and she is not portrayed as morally contaminated merely because she desires him.
For Christians who were raised believing holiness requires pretending sexual desire does not exist, Song of Songs can feel almost scandalous.
But the scandal may not be what Scripture says.
The scandal may be how thoroughly sin has distorted something God created good.
There is an enormous difference between biblical desire and lustful consumption.
Pornography says, “Your body exists for my appetite.”
Biblical love says, “I delight in you.”
Pornography separates bodies from covenant, dignity, faithfulness, sacrifice, and personhood.
Song of Songs refuses to do that.
Its lovers do not speak like consumers browsing bodies.
They speak like people captivated by someone.
That difference matters.
Because Christianity is not a religion teaching that bodies are inherently dirty.
Christianity proclaims something far more astonishing:
“The Word became flesh.”
Jesus Christ did not save humanity by teaching us to escape embodiment. The eternal Son took on a genuine human body. He suffered bodily. He bled bodily. He died bodily. He rose bodily.
And Scripture ultimately promises resurrection.
So when Christians accidentally communicate that physical existence itself is shameful, we are not becoming more biblical.
We are becoming less biblical.
And Song of Songs confronts us with that fact in language many believers never expected to find between Genesis and Revelation.
Listen to Song 4:5 in Hebrew:
שְׁנֵי שָׁדַיִךְ כִּשְׁנֵי עֳפָרִים תְּאוֹמֵי צְבִיָּה הָרוֹעִים בַּשּׁוֹשַׁנִּים
Shenei shadayikh kishnei ‘ofarim, te’omei tseviyyah, haro‘im bashoshanim.
A straightforward translation is:
“Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, grazing among the lilies.”
Yes.
That is actually there.
The Hebrew noun שָׁדַיִךְ — shadayikh — means “your breasts.”
We do Scripture no favors by pretending otherwise.

Later, the poetry becomes even more intensely sensual. The woman’s body is compared with a palm tree and her breasts with clusters. The lover speaks of climbing the palm and taking hold of its branches.
Ancient love poetry communicates through metaphor, fragrance, gardens, fruit, wine, spices, animals, landscape, touch, sight, taste, and longing.
This is poetry.
Beautiful poetry.
Sensual poetry.
And yet there is something profoundly different about its sensuality from the sexual imagery saturating modern culture.
The Song can be explicit without becoming cheap.
Intimate without becoming pornographic.
Sensual without reducing either lover to an object.
There is admiration here.
Mutuality.
Longing.
Exclusivity.
Delight.
The woman can say:
אֲנִי לְדוֹדִי וְעָלַי תְּשׁוּקָתוֹ
Ani ledodi, ve‘alai teshuqato.
“I am my beloved’s, and his desire is for me.”
Notice that word:
תְּשׁוּקָה
teshuqah.
Desire.
Scripture is not frightened by the word.
But Scripture refuses to let desire become god.
And that may be exactly where some of us need conviction.
Because there are two ways Christians can badly misunderstand sexuality.
One is worshiping it.
The other is despising it.
Our culture frequently does the first.
Church culture has sometimes reacted by drifting toward the second.
Neither is biblical.
Sex is a terrible god.
But God's creation is not therefore evil.
Desire can become corrupted, selfish, adulterous, exploitative, obsessive, abusive, pornographic, or idolatrous.
That is why repentance matters.
But corruption does not prove that the original gift was corrupt.
It proves something beautiful has been vandalized.
Genesis tells us that before human shame entered the story, the man and woman were naked and unashamed.
Then sin came.
And suddenly humanity hid.
We have been hiding ever since.
Behind pornography.
Behind promiscuity.
Behind jokes.
Behind shame.
Behind religious performance.
Behind secret browser histories.
Behind marriages where husband and wife have stopped talking honestly.
Behind loneliness.
Behind wounds nobody knows exist.
Some people reading this learned about sex from pornography before anyone trustworthy taught them about God's design.
Some were abused.
Some were betrayed.
Some were taught that sexual desire itself made them filthy.
Some carried questions into adulthood because nobody in church seemed safe enough to ask.
Some entered marriage expecting a wedding ring to instantly erase years of fear and shame.
It didn't.
Some discovered that wounds travel with us.
And some are reading this while carrying secret sin.
You love Jesus.
But there is something you keep returning to when nobody is watching.
A screen.
A fantasy.
A conversation.
A relationship.
A memory.
A hidden appetite.
And afterward comes the familiar collapse.
Delete.
Hide.
Promise.
Cry.
Pray.
Repeat.
Maybe Song of Songs makes you uncomfortable not because Scripture is impure…
but because sin taught us to see sexuality through broken eyes.
Jesus does not call us to pretend desire doesn't exist.
He calls us to holiness.
There is a difference.
Christ does not merely put religious curtains over our darkness.
He brings darkness into the light.

Jesus taught that lust reaches into the heart. He treated adultery seriously. He upheld God's design for marriage. He showed extraordinary mercy toward sexually broken people without ever redefining sin as righteousness.
That combination matters.
Truth without grace crushes wounded people.
Grace without truth leaves wounded people enslaved.
Jesus brings both.
Grace that tells the truth.
Truth that opens the door to grace.

And suddenly Song of Songs begins to feel less like the embarrassing book Christians need to explain away and more like part of God's answer to a world that has forgotten how to distinguish intimacy from consumption.
The Song says beauty can be noticed without becoming merchandise.
Desire can exist without becoming domination.
A woman's longing does not make her dirty.
A man's attraction does not automatically make him predatory.
Bodies are not gods.
Bodies are not garbage.
They are creatures of God.
And sexuality belongs beneath His lordship like everything else.
That means Song of Songs should never become an excuse for lust.
Quite the opposite.
It exposes how counterfeit lust really is.
Pornography promises intimacy while training people for isolation.
It promises satisfaction while cultivating appetite.
It promises connection while turning persons into images.
The Song keeps giving us persons.
“My beloved.”
“My love.”
“My dove.”
Not a category.
Not content.
Not a body detached from a soul.
Beloved.
And there is another important truth Christians should handle carefully.

For centuries, Jewish and Christian readers have also read the Song allegorically. Jewish interpreters have often seen echoes of God's covenant relationship with Israel; Christian interpreters have often heard echoes of Christ's love for His Church. The wider Christian canon certainly gives us a genuine bridegroom-and-bride pattern: Ephesians 5 connects Christian marriage with Christ and the Church.
That theological resonance is beautiful.
But we do not need to erase the Song's ordinary human love poetry to find it.
The safest reading does not force us to choose between “this is genuine love poetry” and “marriage ultimately participates in a larger biblical story.”
Both realities can be respected without pretending every breast, kiss, spice, garden, or fragrance is a secret theological code.
Sometimes a kiss in poetry really is a kiss.
And biblical marriage itself can still point beyond itself.
Paul writes of husband and wife and then says:
There is the greater horizon.
Human marriage is not the Gospel.
But Christian marriage can become a living signpost toward the Gospel.
A bridegroom who loves sacrificially.
A bride who is cherished.
Covenant.
Faithfulness.
Self-giving love.
And above every imperfect human marriage stands the perfect Bridegroom.
Jesus Christ.
This is where the story becomes painfully beautiful.
Because perhaps you haven't loved purely.
Perhaps you crossed boundaries.
Perhaps someone crossed boundaries against you.
Perhaps your marriage has been wounded by betrayal.
Perhaps pornography has hollowed something out inside you.
Perhaps shame has followed you for twenty years.
Perhaps your sexuality feels less like a gift and more like a battlefield.
Perhaps you are single and exhausted from hearing married Christians talk as though marriage were salvation.
Perhaps you have prayed, “Jesus, why is this part of me so difficult to surrender?”
Hear the Gospel carefully.
Jesus did not come only for people whose stories remained clean.
He came for sinners.
People with histories.
People with scars.
People with secrets.
People who have sinned sexually.
People who have sinned relationally.
People whose desires became disordered.
People who were used.
People who used others.
People ashamed of what they have done.
People ashamed of what was done to them.
The cross does not say sin doesn't matter.
The cross says sin mattered enough for Christ to die.
And grace says Christ's sacrifice is sufficient for everyone who comes to Him in repentance and faith.
There is no pornography history stronger than His mercy.
No adultery too sophisticated for Him to expose.
No past relationship capable of overruling His lordship.
No shame permitted to become a greater savior than Jesus.
Repentance does not mean pretending your past never happened.
It means turning from sin toward Christ.
And grace does not merely wipe the courtroom record clean.
Grace begins teaching us how to live differently.
How to see people differently.
How to see bodies differently.
How to love differently.
How to desire without worshiping desire.
How to confess instead of hide.
How to become faithful.
How to receive forgiveness.
How to forgive.
How to stop calling bondage “freedom.”
How to stop calling God's good creation “dirty.”
How to become human again under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
That may be the deepest surprise inside Song of Songs.
Its sensuality is not permission for Christians to become less holy.
It reminds us that holiness is bigger than repression.
Biblical holiness does not require us to mutilate God's creation in our imagination.
It requires us to consecrate ourselves to God.
Everything.
Mind.
Eyes.
Hands.
Relationships.
Marriage.
Singleness.
Longing.
Sexuality.
Memory.
Body.
Future.
Everything belongs to Jesus.
And perhaps somebody needs to hear this tonight:
You do not need another secret.
You need light.
You do not need another promise whispered to yourself at 2:00 a.m.
You need repentance accompanied by whatever concrete obedience repentance requires.
You do not need to hate your body to become holy.
You need to surrender your body to Christ.
You do not need to pretend you never experience temptation.
You need to stop negotiating with it.
And if you have fallen again, do not turn shame into another hiding place.
Run to Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Seek accountability.
Remove access where necessary.
Tell the truth.
Receive mercy.
Get up.
Follow Him again.
The Gospel was never “clean yourself enough and maybe Jesus will accept you.”
The Gospel announces that the holy Son of God came for sinners, died for sins, rose victorious, and calls us to repent, believe, and follow Him.
That changes how we read even the most sensual book in Scripture.
Because Song of Songs does not prove that Christianity secretly celebrates every sexual impulse.
It proves something far richer.
God is not embarrassed by His good creation.
And He refuses to surrender His good creation to sin.
So maybe the question isn't:
“Why is this sensual book in the Bible?”
Maybe the better question is:
“What happened to us that made pornography seem normal while faithful marital delight became embarrassing?”
That question hurts.
It should.
Because Christians cannot disciple a sexually broken generation merely by saying “don't.”
We must show them the greater “yes.”
Yes to covenant.
Yes to dignity.
Yes to faithfulness.
Yes to seeing another human being as an image-bearer rather than consumable content.
Yes to repentance.
Yes to forgiveness.
Yes to healing.
Yes to marriages where affection does not need to apologize for existing.
Yes to singleness that is fully human and fully capable of holiness, purpose, intimacy with God, friendship, service, and joy.
Yes to bodies submitted to Christ.
Yes to grace stronger than yesterday.
And ultimately…
Yes to Jesus.
The Bridegroom who does not exploit His Bride.
He gives Himself for her.
The One who does not consume.
He sacrifices.
The One who sees every hidden stain and nevertheless moves toward repentant sinners with cleansing grace.
This is why Ephesians tells husbands:
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
There is the Christian revolution.
The world's counterfeit says:
Take.
Christ says:
Give yourself.
The world's counterfeit asks:
How can this person satisfy me?
Christlike love asks:
How can I faithfully seek this person's good?
The world's counterfeit turns desire into entitlement.
Jesus turns love toward sacrifice.
And suddenly the Bible's vision of sexuality becomes more demanding than both promiscuity and repression.
It asks for holy desire.
Faithful desire.
Humanizing desire.
Covenantal love.
Self-control.
Sacrifice.
Tenderness.
Truth.
And grace when sinners fail.
Maybe that is why Song of Songs still makes us uncomfortable.
It refuses our easy categories.
It is sensual but not pornographic.
Physical but not materialistic.
Passionate but not promiscuous.
Poetic but remarkably candid.
Human while sitting inside a canon whose ultimate story leads us to Jesus Christ.
And perhaps the person who most needs this article isn't you.
Maybe it is the husband silently fighting pornography.
The wife who believes her body is undesirable.
The teenager receiving theology from TikTok and sexuality from explicit content.
The single Christian ashamed of having sexual desire at all.
The believer convinced a sexual past permanently disqualified them from being loved by God.
The couple who cannot speak honestly anymore.
The friend hiding an affair.
The wounded person who has confused what someone did to them with who they are.
Send this to them.
Not as ammunition.
Not as judgment.
As an open door toward Scripture, honesty, repentance, healing, and Jesus.
If this exposed something you've been hiding, comment, “Jesus, heal what sin distorted.”
If shame has kept you silent for years, comment, “No more hiding.”

And if Christ has already begun restoring an area of your life you once thought could never be redeemed, tell that testimony. Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that grace still reaches people like them.
Not because paying for something earns favor with God.
It doesn't.
Not because Christians can purchase spiritual blessing.
They cannot.
It doesn't.
We glorify God through faith and obedience to Christ.
But supporting Gospel-centered ministry can be one practical expression of generosity when it is done freely, prayerfully, and without compulsion.
Share because someone may need the truth.
Tag because someone you love may be hiding.
Save because temptation has a way of making us forget what we knew in the light.
Follow because none of us outgrows our need for Scripture.
But above all of it—
Follow Jesus.
Because the goal was never building an audience around Gospel Warrior.
The goal is pointing an audience toward Christ.

And when every screen goes dark, every platform disappears, every hidden browser history is exposed, every human body returns to dust, and every earthly love reaches its limit, there will still be One whose grace has the final word over every sinner who belongs to Him.
Maybe that is what you needed to hear more than anything else.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
The God who placed passionate poetry inside Scripture is neither embarrassed by your humanity nor permissive toward your sin.
He calls you out of hiding.
He calls you into truth.
He calls you to repentance.
He calls you to grace.
He calls you to Himself.
And when Jesus takes hold of a surrendered life, even the places sin tried hardest to vandalize can become places where redemption tells the louder story.
Sin may have written scandal across the page, but surrendered to Christ, scandal does not get to write the ending.
